820.title: Elizabeth of Hungary
820.hook: a young noblewoman who spent her fortune on a hospital; legend says bread turned to roses
820.howItsDone: Catholics, Lutherans and Anglicans honor Elizabeth of Hungary, and among hospitals, charities and parishes named for her, some of them mark her feast day with bread or food for the poor.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Dominic's preachers, who took it in and gave it away, and your line was to contemplate and to share.

A young woman hurries down from a castle with her cloak held closed. Underneath is bread, a lot of it, for the hungry people waiting below. Someone stops her on the path; in some tellings it's her husband, in others a suspicious relative. What are you carrying? She can't hide it, so she opens the cloak, and what falls out, the legend says, is roses. That's the story people tell about Elizabeth of Hungary, a king's daughter who married into a noble German house. The roses are a legend. The bread is not.

Elizabeth was born to Hungary's royal family and sent as a girl to the court of Thuringia, in Germany, to marry Louis, the son of its ruler, who later ruled there himself. The early accounts say the marriage was a loving one. They also say she wasn't a comfortable person to have at a royal table. She refused food she believed had been taken unjustly from the poor. In a time of hunger she gave out grain from the stores, and she went down to the sick herself. Then her husband died, away from home, on his way to a crusade, and her life changed fast. She left court and took up a life of poverty, close to the Franciscans. With what was left of her fortune she built a hospital at Marburg, and worked in it: washing, feeding, sitting with people others avoided. Behind this is a passage in Matthew. When the Son of man comes in his glory, the king tells people, "For I was an hungred, and ye gave me meat." Whatever they did for the least of his family, they did for him. In the Gospel's own terms, feeding the hungry is serving Christ. In the Gospels' Greek, bread is artos, the same word as in the prayer, give us this day our daily bread. And the roses? Some hear a miracle, some a picture: what you give in secret becomes beautiful. Either way, the story keeps her as she was, caught on the path, holding bread for someone else.
screen: `A KING'S DAUGHTER AT A GERMAN COURT.`

segments.voice: Think of someone who could use bread this week, in any form: a sick neighbor, a coworker who skips lunch, a shelter or food bank near you. Let one face or place come, and picture bringing it, nothing hidden. If you pray, hold that person in prayer; if not, hold them in mind.
Elizabeth. A king's daughter of Hungary who fed the hungry, served the sick at a hospital she built, and, legend says, carried bread that became roses.
Your line: bread into roses. A cloak full of bread, held open. Eight hundred twenty days in.

821.title: The dumb ox
821.hook: Thomas Aquinas was so quiet at school they called him the dumb ox
821.tomorrow: Aquinas: it all seems like straw
821.howItsDone: Catholics honor Thomas Aquinas as a saint and a Doctor of the Church, and his writings are studied in Catholic seminaries and universities and by readers of other churches too.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Elizabeth, with bread under her cloak, and your line was bread into roses.

In a lecture hall in Cologne sits a big student who almost never speaks. He listens, he writes, he doesn't argue in class. The other students decide he can't be very bright, and they give him a nickname: the dumb ox. One classmate feels sorry for him and offers to go over the lessons with him. The big student says yes, thank you, and sits while the classmate explains. Then the classmate gets tangled in a hard passage. And the quiet one, gently, explains the whole thing, clearly, start to finish. The student is Thomas Aquinas.

Thomas had already paid a price to be in that room. His noble Italian family had other plans for him, and when he joined Dominic's preachers, the friars from two days ago, his family stopped him on the road and kept him at home for a long time, trying to change his mind. They couldn't. Now here he is in Cologne, studying under a famous teacher, Albert, later called Albert the Great. What happened next comes from Thomas's early biographer, William of Tocco. Albert gives the class a hard question and has Thomas answer it in public. He does, so clearly that Albert turns to the room: you call him the dumb ox, but this ox will one day bellow so loud the whole world will hear. Notice what the quiet was. Not emptiness: attention. He wasn't speaking because he was listening, all the way down. And notice how he took the classmate's offer: no correction, no showing off, just yes, thank you. The letter of James puts it plainly, in the King James Bible: "let every man be swift to hear, slow to speak." Later Thomas would write a great deal, and Christians still read him, argue with him and learn from him. But it started with a young man nobody thought much of, sitting in the back, listening. The loudest voice in the room isn't always the one that understands.

Bring to mind someone in your life who doesn't say much, at work, at the table, in a group chat where they only ever send a thumbs up. Wonder for a moment what they notice that the rest of you miss, and what they've never been asked. If you pray, give thanks for them; if not, let your respect for them grow a little.
Dumb ox. The nickname classmates gave Thomas Aquinas because he was quiet. His teacher Albert said the ox would one day bellow.
Your line: the ox will bellow. Quiet is not the same as empty. Day eight hundred twenty-one.

822.title: Aquinas: it all seems like straw
822.hook: after an experience at Mass he stopped writing, saying all his work seemed like straw
822.howItsDone: Catholic students and teachers still study the Summa Theologiae, and the story of the straw is told in retreats and sermons about the limits of words before God.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the dumb ox, the quiet student in the back, and your line was the ox will bellow.

Straw. That's the word he used. The quiet student has grown into a great teacher. For years he has been writing a vast work explaining the Christian faith, question by question, dictating to helpers. Then one morning in Naples he says Mass, and something happens. The sources never say what. Afterward he puts down his pen. He won't write or dictate. His friend and companion, Reginald, begs him to go on, and Thomas gives a strange answer.

The account comes from testimony gathered after his death, when the church was looking into his life. Reginald presses him: why stop now? And Thomas says, in effect: I can't. Everything I have written seems like straw to me, compared with what I have seen. That's the whole story. He never says what he saw, or explains it, or teaches it. The great work, the one people still call the Summa, is left unfinished, and he dies not long after, on a journey. What do you do with that? First, notice what he didn't say. He didn't say his work was false, or burn it. Straw isn't poison. Straw is what grain grows on; it holds the wheat up, and then the harvest is gathered and the straw left in the field. The church kept reading him, and still does. Second, notice where it happened: at Mass, in prayer, not at a desk. Thomas spent his life using reason to speak about God, and believed reason was a gift. But Paul had already said our knowing has a limit: "For now we see through a glass, darkly; but then face to face." Some readers hear in the straw a man who glimpsed the face. Some wonder whether he was ill or worn out, and say both could be true. The sources don't settle it. They leave a teacher who stopped talking, and a silence where the rest of his book should be.
screen: `STRAW, COMPARED WITH WHAT I HAVE SEEN.`

segments.voice: Put down whatever you're holding, the phone, the pen, the plan for the next hour, and for this minute add no words of your own, letting each thought go by like a cart on a far road. If you pray, you can sit with a line from the prophet Habakkuk, let all the earth keep silence before him; if not, let the quiet be full.
Aquinas. Thomas Aquinas, the teacher who explained the faith question by question, and then stopped writing, saying it all seemed like straw beside what he had seen.
Your line: all is straw. Straw isn't poison; it holds the wheat up. Until tomorrow.

823.title: Bonaventure's journey
823.hook: the Franciscan who saw every creature as a step toward God
823.howItsDone: Franciscans and other Christians read Bonaventure's Journey of the Mind into God slowly, often on retreat, and some practice prayerful walks in nature that follow its first steps.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Aquinas put down his pen and called it all straw, and your line was all is straw.

What would it take to see a sparrow as a staircase? A Franciscan friar named Bonaventure climbs a mountain in Italy called La Verna. It's where, the story goes, Francis had a vision near the end of his life: a fiery angel, a seraph, with six wings. Bonaventure has a heavy job by now: he leads the whole family of Franciscan brothers. He goes up, he says, looking for peace. And while he's there, thinking about Francis's vision, an idea comes that becomes a small book.

The book is called The Journey of the Mind into God. Bonaventure reads the six wings as six steps. The soul climbs, he says, like going up a ladder, and the first rungs are right under your feet: the things God made. A stone, a river, a sparrow. Each carries a trace of the one who made it, the way a footprint in the sand tells you someone walked there. Then you climb inward, to your own mind, where he finds God's image. Then upward, beyond what the mind can hold. But it starts with creatures. Behind that is a line from Romans, in the King James Bible: "For the invisible things of him from the creation of the world are clearly seen, being understood by the things that are made." Francis is close behind it, the man whose song made the sun a brother. Bonaventure gives that love a map. Every creature is a step: not a stopping place, not something to grab, but a step on the way up. By the stories told about him, he was a humble climber. Tradition says that when messengers came to tell him the pope had made him a cardinal, they found him washing dishes, and he asked them to hang the cardinal's hat on a tree until he finished. Whether or not it went that way, it's the kind of story told about a man who saw holy things in ordinary places. A dish. A tree. A sparrow on a fence.
screen: `SEEN BY THE THINGS THAT ARE MADE.`

segments.voice: Find one living thing you can see from where you are, a plant, a bird outside, even your own hand, and look at it as if it were the first of its kind you'd ever seen. Then let your attention rise a little, past it, toward whatever made it, however you name that. If you pray, give thanks for this one creature; if not, let the looking be thanks enough.
Bonaventure's journey. His book The Journey of the Mind into God: climbing from the things God made, inward to the mind, and upward to God.
Your line: every creature a step. Not a stopping place, but a rung. Step by step, day eight hundred twenty-three.

824.title: The Beguines
824.hook: lay women living together to pray and serve in medieval cities, like Mechthild of Magdeburg
824.howItsDone: Some beguinages in Belgium and the Netherlands still stand and can be visited, and Christian lay communities today, women's and mixed, still live together to pray and serve their neighborhoods.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Bonaventure's journey up the ladder of creatures, and your line was every creature a step.

Inside a medieval city, behind a wall and a gate, there's a little town of its own: small houses around a green, a chapel, a garden. Women come back in the evening from nursing the sick, or sit at a loom, or teach children their letters. At night the gate closes, and the bell rings for prayer. These women are not nuns. They haven't taken vows for life, and some could leave tomorrow and marry. But for now they've chosen to live here together, to pray, to work and to serve the city around them.

The Beguines grew up in the cities of what is now Belgium, the Netherlands and Germany. They were lay women, ordinary Christians, who wanted the gospel life without entering a convent. They lived in shared houses or walled courts called beguinages, earned their living with their hands, cared for the sick and the dying, and prayed together. Their picture of life together goes back to the first Christians in Jerusalem, in Acts, in the King James Bible: "And all that believed were together, and had all things common." The Greek word for in common there is koina. One Beguine became a writer. Mechthild of Magdeburg lived as a Beguine in that German city and wrote a book called The Flowing Light of the Godhead, in German, the language of the street, not Latin. It's full of love talk between the soul and God, bold and tender. In one passage she says, in effect, that a fish can't drown in water and a bird can't sink in the air, and the soul is made to live in God the same way. Not everyone was comfortable with women living like this, outside the usual rules, praying and writing in their own words. Church leaders at times grew suspicious, and some Beguines were investigated or condemned. Mechthild herself, late in life, went to live with nuns at a convent called Helfta. But the beguinages lasted, and you can still walk through some today. Women, together, in the middle of the city.

Think of the people who live nearest you, on your street or in your building, not one at a time but together. Let one small thing come that you could do alongside them, not just for them: a cleanup, a meal train, checking on an older neighbor. If you pray, hold your street in prayer; if not, hold the faces you know there.
The Beguines. Lay women in medieval cities who lived together, without lifelong vows, to pray, work with their hands and serve the sick.
Your line: women together. Praying, working, serving, side by side. Day eight hundred twenty-four is yours.

825.title: Dante's journey
825.hook: midway through life's journey, lost in a dark wood, Dante is led by love through hell, purgatory and heaven
825.carry: the love that moves the sun
825.howItsDone: Christians and other readers take up Dante's Divine Comedy as poetry and as a spiritual journey, and some churches and reading groups go through it slowly, a canto at a time.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Beguines, living side by side behind a city gate, and your line was women together.

In the middle of the journey of our life, I found myself in a dark wood, for the straight way was lost. That's how a long Christian poem begins, put into plain English. A man halfway through his life wakes up lost, with no idea how he got there. The wood is wild and thick. He sees a hill with sunlight on it and tries to climb, and wild animals drive him back down. He is stuck. Then someone appears to help. The man is the poet Dante, writing about himself.

The poem is known as the Divine Comedy. The help that comes in the wood is the ghost of Virgil, an old Roman poet, sent because Beatrice, a woman Dante loved who has died, asked for him. So the journey starts with love reaching down into the dark. Virgil leads Dante down through hell, where people are stuck forever in the shape of their choices. Then up a mountain, purgatory, where souls are being healed and made ready, climbing slowly, even singing. Then Beatrice herself guides him up through the heavens. The way out of the dark wood isn't straight up the sunny hill. It goes down first, and only then up. The poem is honest about pain. In heaven, Dante's ancestor tells him what's coming: he'll be driven out of his city, Florence. He'll learn how salty another man's bread tastes, and how hard it is to climb another man's stairs. Then the last line. Dante sees God, and can't describe it. All he can say is that his desire and will were turned, like a wheel, by "l'amor che move il sole e l'altre stelle." The love that moves the sun and the other stars. The poem began in a dark wood. It ends at the center of everything, with love. Christians read it in different ways: as a story, a map of the soul, a vision.

Ask quietly where you are on your own journey, in a dark wood, going down through something hard, climbing slowly, or somewhere bright, and name it in a word or two, with nothing to fix. Then ask who has been your Virgil, someone who helped you find the way. If you pray, bring that place and that person to God; if not, hold them both for a moment.
Dante's journey. A poet lost in a dark wood, led by love down through hell, up the mountain of purgatory, and into heaven.
Your line: the love that moves the sun. The dark wood was only the beginning. On to tomorrow.

826.title: Palamas and the uncreated light
826.hook: on Mount Athos, monks praying the Jesus Prayer say they see the light of Tabor
826.howItsDone: Orthodox Christians, and some Catholics and Protestants, pray the Jesus Prayer, often with a prayer rope, and Orthodox churches keep a Sunday in Lent in memory of Gregory Palamas.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Dante's journey from a dark wood to heaven, and your line was the love that moves the sun.

Night on Mount Athos, a rocky peninsula in Greece, home to monks. In a small cell, a monk sits on a low stool, head bowed, breathing slowly. With each breath he says the same short prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God, have mercy on me. Hours go by. And some of these monks say that in the stillness they see light. Not a lamp, not the moon: a light they say is God's own, the same light the disciples saw on Mount Tabor. Others laughed at them. Today's word is what the monks were doing.

Hesychasm. When Paul tells one church, in the King James Bible, to "study to be quiet," the Greek verb he uses is from the same family: hesychazo, to be still. Hesychasts are the people of stillness. Their prayer, the Jesus Prayer, grows out of cries in the Gospels: the tax collector's "God be merciful to me a sinner," and the blind man's "Jesus, thou son of David, have mercy on me." Said slowly, with the breath. And the light? They point to the Transfiguration. Jesus takes three disciples up a mountain, tradition says Tabor, and there, Matthew writes, "his face did shine as the sun, and his raiment was white as the light." The monks say that light can still be seen. A learned man named Barlaam mocked them: God can't be seen with bodily eyes, so whatever you're seeing, it isn't God. A monk of Athos, Gregory Palamas, answered with a distinction. God's essence, what God is in himself, is beyond every creature, forever. But God's energies, his life, his grace, his light, are truly God too, uncreated, and God gives them. So a person can really share in God's light without swallowing up God's mystery. Church councils in Constantinople sided with Palamas, and Orthodox Christians honor him as a saint. Western churches have read his ideas in different ways, and theologians still discuss them. For the people of stillness, the quiet was never empty. It was a cell kept ready for light.
